source.title: Scaling Laws for Imitation Learning in Single-Agent Games
source.authors: Jens Tuyls; Dhruv Madeka; K. Torkkola; Dean Phillips Foster; Karthik Narasimhan; S. Kakade

record.tranche_reason: Extends scaling-law analyses to behavioral cloning and reinforcement learning in Atari and NetHack games, using held-out imitation loss and compute-optimal model/data allocation.
record.gate_note: The study tests game-agent scaling, not language-model pretraining. Its fitting and forecasting results are included only as tests in imitation learning or RL; no cited language-model result is recorded as a row.
record.test_reason: The study applies Kaplan/Hoffmann-style isoFLOP and parametric scaling-law fits to behavioral cloning (Atari CNNs, NetHack Transformers) and to RL (NetHack IMPALA). It reports power-law fits for loss, optimal model and data size, and return, compares two fitting methods, and checks one forecast. Its own results bear on V5 (a new training regime) and on V7 (fitting-method dependence). V1–V3, V4 and V6 name language-model pretraining, which the study does not train.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially right but omits two points. The authors conclude that IL loss and mean return follow power laws in FLOPs across Atari and NetHack and are highly correlated. They report that scaling-law forecasts produce compute-optimal NetHack agents that beat the prior offline SOTA by 1.7x. They also find similar power laws for model size and interactions in a brief NetHack RL study. They note uncertainty in the coefficients from using a constant learning rate, and that partial observability may affect the laws.
record.recipe_differences: Uses isoFLOP profiles and a parametric fit inspired by Hoffmann et al., but studies behavioral cloning/RL on game trajectories and action prediction rather than language-model token prediction. The data axis is samples or environment interactions, not tokens.
record.method_sensitivity: For NetHack BC, loss-optimal parameter/sample exponents are similar between isoFLOP and parametric fitting, while return-optimal exponents differ. Forecast models use a cosine learning-rate schedule; isoFLOP profiles use a constant rate. Context length and inventory feature availability also change validation loss.

fits_no_version.finding: NetHack game return is strongly correlated with optimal BC loss and follows an inverse power law plus constant; Atari shows the same.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In single-agent games, environment return improves smoothly with imitation loss.

fits_no_version.finding: Longer NetHack context improves BC loss up to 4096, then gains are marginal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For NetHack imitation, access to longer history improves expert-action prediction.

fits_no_version.finding: Including inventory features improves NetHack BC loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Information parity with the expert improves imitation loss.

fits_no_version.finding: Dev loss varies only ~0.223–0.230 across width/depth aspect ratios 0–300 for 40M–105M NetHack Transformers (axis ticks; figure only); the best ratio is a little over 100 at all sizes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In NetHack BC Transformers, the loss-optimal aspect ratio is stable across model size and loss is insensitive to shape.

record.problems: The authors state that they used a constant learning rate across isoFLOP runs to reduce compute, despite recommendations for separate schedules, and acknowledge uncertainty in fitted coefficients. The RL isoFLOP sweep has one seed per point and is described as noisy. Atari held-out sets contain about 100 trajectories, and only eight Atari games were tested. The study does not compare scaling coefficients across architectures or environments in a controlled way.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant rows were omitted. Appendix plots contain per-game fitted curves; r2 records the paper's explicit aggregate statement for Atari rather than transcribing every plotted fit.

untested.parts: No language-model pretraining loss is measured.
No LM extrapolation. The game-agent forecast extends less than one order of magnitude in compute.
No LM parameter/token allocation. The game-agent allocation exponents are recorded under V5.
No LM shape sweep at fixed parameters; only an aspect-ratio tuning sweep in NetHack BC.
Image/video generative modelling, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer are not tested.
No downstream LM tasks. Game return vs loss (r17) is a related but different construct.
Parameter-counting and data choices are not varied. The learning-rate schedule effect on the fitted laws is only speculated about.

missing.what: RL parametric fit gives α=0.6, β=0.4 (low-FLOP budgets dropped) vs isoFLOP α=0.43, β=0.56. Human-level forecasts differ: 4.4B params/13.2T interactions vs 67B/0.93T.

Return forecasts at 40B (32M params) and 55B (45M params): the models performed a bit better than predicted, possibly due to the cosine vs constant learning-rate schedule. The best agent scores 7784 on Human Monk.
Per-game Atari exponents vary widely: loss-optimal α 0.58–0.79 and β 0.34–0.51; return-optimal α 0.21–0.88, with Phoenix not significant.

record.verdict_notes: V1–V4 and V6 are treated as LM-specific, so game-agent allocation, shape and return results go under V5 or fits_no_version. V7 is treated as a general methodological claim. The reader's V3 labels are dropped, and the V4 limits_scope is dropped because it is not a test of V4. The r10 V7 link in the record's V7 label is removed.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure held-out language-model pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
The forecasting experiments concern imitation-learning agents, not language-model runs.
Tests allocation between model parameters and demonstration samples for imitation learning, not language-model parameters and training tokens.
Tests an aspect-ratio sweep for NetHack models, but does not establish loss changes at fixed parameter count across a wide range of depth, width, and other architecture choices.
Tests behavioral cloning and briefly RL in single-agent games; it does not test image/video generative pretraining, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Reports game return in relation to imitation loss, not downstream-task performance of language models.
Shows fitting-method and schedule differences in its own game-agent experiments; it does not test whether language-model exponents or published language-model laws depend on these choices.
